cards.explanation: The answer is cherubim. They are skillfully worked right into the curtains (Exodus 36:8). That's not a sticker slapped on after the fact, friends. The craftsmen built them into the linen and the blue, purple and scarlet yarn. I once bent a whole batch of cookies trying to make a star look like a star, so I'm impressed.

The answer is that the clasps join it into one unit. The fifty gold clasps join the curtains together, “…so that the tabernacle was a unit.” (Exodus 36:13). Two sets of five curtains go in, and one tabernacle comes out. Fifty little gold clasps holding it all together, and I can't even keep my apron strings tied on a humid day.

The answer is six. The eleven goat hair curtains are joined into one set of five and another of six (Exodus 36:16). Five plus six makes eleven. I counted them off with my mustache, twice, because I don't trust my own math.

The answer is fifty. Each set of goat hair curtains gets fifty loops along its edge (Exodus 36:17). The linen curtains also had fifty loops (Exodus 36:12). Fifty again, so keep that number handy, friends.

The answer is True, friends! The veil is made of blue, purple and scarlet yarn and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it (Exodus 36:35). The ten curtains got the same treatment (Exodus 36:8). Same fancy yarn, same cherubim. I once spent a whole afternoon getting one cookie to come out straight, and these folks are working cherubim into cloth.

The answer is silver. The veil's four posts are acacia wood overlaid with gold, and the craftsman cast four silver bases for them (Exodus 36:36). Gold on top and silver on the bottom. The posts are dressed up from head to toe.

The answer is bronze. The entrance has five posts with their hooks, and their five bases were bronze (Exodus 36:38). The veil's posts sit on silver (Exodus 36:36), so the metal changes at the door. Silver inside, bronze at the entrance.

The answer is carrying the ark. Bezalel, the lead craftsman, makes poles of acacia wood overlaid with gold, and he puts them into the rings on the sides of the ark in order to carry it (Exodus 37:4-5). The gold rings and gold poles are built in from the start. The ark is made to be carried.

The answer is a cherub, one on each end of the mercy seat. Both are hammered gold, and both are made from one piece of gold (Exodus 37:7-8). Hammered, not stuck on. That is a lot of patience with a hammer.

The answer is True, friends! The cherubim have wings that spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat, and they face each other, looking toward the mercy seat (Exodus 37:9). Two gold figures, wings up, facing each other. I can't even keep my eyes on one cookie.

The answer is plates and bowls and pitchers. The utensils for the table are pure gold: plates and dishes, as well as bowls and pitchers for pouring drink offerings (Exodus 37:16). All pure gold, no plain metal in the bunch. My cookie sheets are jealous.

The answer is almond. Each branch gets three cups shaped like almond blossoms, each with buds and petals (Exodus 37:19). That's a lampstand with flowers hammered right into the gold. A lot of detail for something that holds lamps.

The answer is False, friends. Nobody is gluing anything on here. The buds and branches were all of one piece with the lampstand, hammered out of pure gold (Exodus 37:22). Verse 17 says the whole lampstand is all of one piece (Exodus 37:17). If I had to hammer that from a single lump, I'd have flat gold and a very sore mustache.

The answer is seven. Bezalel also made its seven lamps, its wick trimmers and trays of pure gold (Exodus 37:23). The lamps, trimmers and trays are all pure gold. Seven lamps up there, and I just try to keep one oven light working.

The answer is burning incense. The text calls it the altar of incense (Exodus 37:25), and Bezalel also made the pure, fragrant incense (Exodus 37:29). It's small and square, overlaid with pure gold, with horns that were of one piece with it. A little altar with a lot of gold.

The answer is a horn. Bezalel makes a horn at each of the altar's four corners, and the horns and the altar are of one piece (Exodus 38:2). The horns are part of the altar itself, not an add-on. Four corners, four horns.

The answer is bronze. Bezalel overlaid the altar of burnt offering with bronze (Exodus 38:2), and all its utensils are bronze too (Exodus 38:3). The little altar of incense got gold, but this big one gets bronze. Different altar, different metal.

The answer is True. Bezalel cast four rings for the bronze grate and made poles of acacia wood overlaid with bronze. He inserted the poles into the rings on the sides of the altar for carrying it (Exodus 38:5-7). Same plan as the ark and the table. The poles are bronze this time instead of gold.

The answer is False. The text says, “He made the altar with boards so that it was hollow.” (Exodus 38:7). It's built with boards, with room inside. That's one big hollow altar, and I wish my cookie jar were that roomy.

The answer is the mirrors of the serving women. Bezalel made the bronze basin and its stand from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (Exodus 38:8). Nobody would have guessed that one. Shiny mirrors turned into a bronze basin.

The answer is Judah. The inventory says Bezalel is of the tribe of Judah (Exodus 38:22). It even gives his family line: son of Uri, the son of Hur. I think that's a proud name to have written next to yours, while all I've got is “Dorin” carved on my handle.

The answer is Dan. Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, was with Bezalel as an engraver, designer and embroiderer in blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine linen (Exodus 38:23). That's a long job title for one man. Two tribes working side by side.
